advisor.summary: An aircraft used predominantly in a real trade or business supports very large deductions — operating costs under §162 and cost recovery including permanent 100 percent bonus — and draws more concentrated IRS attention than anything else in this library. It is §280F listed property demanding more-than-50-percent qualified business use proven flight by flight; entertainment use disallows a proportionate share of every cost including depreciation under the occupied-seat rules; personal flights by owners impute income under the SIFL formula; and LB&I has run a dedicated business-aircraft audit campaign since February 2024. The engine deducts a single advisor-supplied figure from the separate depreciation and cost study — this strategy must never be presented without that study underneath it, and the file should be built as if the exam notice were already in the mail.
mechanics: Deductibility begins with §162: recurring business transportation needs that commercial schedules serve poorly — multi-site operations, dispersed clients, time-critical work — documented per flight with route, passengers, and purpose.

Aircraft are listed property under §280F(d)(4): accelerated and bonus depreciation require qualified business use above 50 percent in every year of the recovery period, and a failing year triggers recapture plus straight-line ADS going forward.

Entertainment use is carved out by Reg. §1.274-10: all costs, depreciation included, are allocated across occupied seats flight by flight, and the entertainment share is disallowed even when income is imputed to the executive.

Personal non-entertainment flights by owner-employees impute compensation under the SIFL rules of Reg. §1.61-21(g) — payroll must actually run the numbers, and the deduction-versus-compensation mismatch is a standing exam adjustment.
Where profit motive is thin, §183 caps the activity's deductions; owner-to-business leasing structures layer §469 self-rental and state sales-and-use issues that need their own analysis.

The model applies one number — the annual business-use deduction from the separate study — as an entity deduction; depreciation schedules, entertainment disallowance, and SIFL all live in that study, not in the engine.

authority.note: Ordinary and necessary is the foundation — the business case for each flight.
Listed-property status: the more-than-50-percent qualified-business-use test, recapture, and ADS on failure.
Permanent 100 percent bonus on qualifying aircraft acquired after January 19, 2025 — the number that makes year one enormous.
Occupied-seat allocation and disallowance of the entertainment share of all aircraft costs, including depreciation.
The SIFL valuation formula for imputing personal flights to owner-employees.
Hobby-loss and passive/self-rental limits on structures without a solid profit motive.
The LB&I business-aircraft audit campaign — the reason this file is built exam-first.

requirements: A genuine, recurring transportation need that commercial travel serves poorly — provable with routes and schedules, not adjectives.
Qualified business use above 50 percent, evidenced by contemporaneous flight-by-flight logs.
A separate depreciation and operating-cost study producing the annual deduction the model applies.
SIFL imputation running in payroll and the annual entertainment-use allocation computed.
FAA, insurance, and state sales-and-use coordination handled outside this model.
risks: Elevated audit probability is not a maybe: the LB&I campaign announced in IR-2024-46 targets exactly this deduction, and the leading theory is personal and entertainment use dressed as business — build the position assuming examination.
One personal-heavy flying season can gut the year: the occupied-seat allocation disallows a proportionate share of all costs, bonus depreciation included.
Business use at or below 50 percent in any recovery-period year triggers listed-property recapture and ADS going forward.
Missed SIFL imputation stacks a payroll-tax exposure on top of the income-tax adjustment.
Weak profit motive invites §183 recharacterization, and the economics rarely pencil on tax savings alone — the aircraft must make business sense before tax.
stateNotes: Conformity: state depreciation decoupling hits hardest here — a bonus-decoupled state spreads the headline deduction over years, and state sales-and-use tax on the acquisition is frequently the largest non-federal number in the deal.
PTET interaction: the deduction reduces electing-entity income before any pass-through entity tax computation; a swing this large mandates a PTET estimate reset.

Missouri: conforms to federal bonus through rolling conformity (RSMo §143.091); Missouri sales/use tax on the acquisition and any owner-to-entity lease should be scoped with the state filings before closing.
reviewChecklist: The separate aircraft study exists, is current, and its number is what the model applies — no study, no strategy.
Flight logs reviewed: route, passengers, and per-seat purpose classification for every flight.
Business-use percentage above 50 percent with margin, not at the line.
SIFL entries confirmed in payroll and the entertainment allocation reconciled.
Client has signed off on the audit posture and the documentation burden in writing.

client.teaser: A serious deduction for a serious business tool — with rules to match.
client.headline: When the plane is a business tool, the tax law treats it like one
plainEnglish: If your business truly depends on private air travel — several locations, clients spread across the map, schedules airlines cannot meet — the tax law allows real deductions. Operating costs of business flights count. So can a very large first-year write-off on the aircraft itself.

This is also one of the most closely watched deductions in the tax code. The IRS runs a dedicated audit program for business aircraft. Every flight needs a log showing who was aboard and why. Personal trips get added to your income at set rates, and vacation-style flights cancel part of the deduction.

None of that is a reason to walk away. It is a reason to do it properly. We make sure the numbers come from a real study, the records start with the first flight, and the deduction we claim is one we can defend without flinching.
client.analogy: Think of it as a company truck, times a thousand. The write-off is bigger — and so is the paperwork that has to ride along.
